name: Harbor blue
lede: Harbor blue is a muted, greenish [[blue]] whose name is undocumented: our sources record the color but not who named it or why.

sections.title: A blue with no traced origin
sections.body:
Our data carries this name from the 2010 xkcd crowd survey, and separately from Maerz and Paul's 1930 color dictionary, as cited by the ISCC-NBS circular of 1955, but neither source explains the choice of "harbor" [1]. In the ISCC-NBS system it falls nearest the block called "strong greenish blue", 4.5 units off [2]. In Munsell terms it reads about 7.6B 5.0/5.8, a mid-toned, moderately saturated blue leaning toward green [2].

The word suggests the grey-green water of a sheltered port rather than open ocean or sky, but that reading is ours, not a traced etymology [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[chessylite-blue]], [[beaucaire]] and [[faience]], at 2.8, 3.2 and 4.3 ΔE [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 53 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.2 percent, as photographed [3]. The earliest dated match is Gerard David's *Lamentation over the Body of Christ*, from about 1490, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. Its clearest peak is the 1900s, at roughly four and a half times the archive's overall rate [3]. [[painter:claude-monet|Claude Monet]] used it far more than most painters, at about 45 times the baseline rate, including in his 1882 *[[painting:cma-125234|Low Tide at Pourville, near Dieppe]]* [3]. [[painter:john-singer-sargent|John Singer Sargent]] also reached for it, in works such as his 1892 *[[painting:commons-Q20771658|Pagan Deities]]* [3]. On the same canvases it most often keeps company with [[slate]] [3]. These counts are computed color matches on photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [3].
